::: {.callout-note}
## Reading
- **Compulsory:** @strogatz2024nonlinear, Section 7.5 on relaxation oscillators.
- **Recommended:** @ellner2006dynamic, chapter on neural and excitable dynamics.
:::

A system is **excitable** if it has a stable rest state, small perturbations decay back to rest, and perturbations above a threshold produce a large excursion before the system returns to rest. Nerve cells behave this way: a small current injection changes the membrane potential slightly, while a larger one triggers an action potential [@hodgkin1952quantitative; @strogatz2024nonlinear].

## Background: the Hodgkin-Huxley model

Hodgkin and Huxley described the membrane potential $V$ of the squid giant axon with four ODEs: one for $V$ and three for gating variables $m$, $h$, $n$ that control the sodium and potassium conductances [@hodgkin1952quantitative]:

$$
C\dot V = I - \bar g_{\text{Na}} m^3 h (V - V_{\text{Na}}) - \bar g_{\text{K}} n^4 (V - V_{\text{K}}) - g_L (V - V_L),
$$

with each gating variable relaxing to a voltage-dependent steady state. The model reproduced the shape and speed of the action potential measured in experiments. Hodgkin and Huxley shared the [1963 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1963/summary/) with John Eccles, for discoveries on the ionic mechanisms of excitation and inhibition in nerve cell membranes.

Four variables are hard to analyse geometrically. The two-variable models of this session keep the essential structure and can be studied in the phase plane [@fitzhugh1961impulses; @morris1981voltage].

## The ingredients

- A **fast variable** (membrane potential) with an S-shaped, or cubic, nullcline. The middle branch has positive feedback: a small depolarization opens channels that depolarize further.
- A **slow recovery variable** that eventually pulls the fast variable back.
- A **separation of time scales**: the fast variable changes much faster than the slow one, so trajectories jump quickly between the outer branches of the cubic nullcline and drift slowly along them [@strogatz2024nonlinear, Section 7.5].

The threshold is not a sharp number in general. In FitzHugh's analysis it is a narrow band in the phase plane near the middle branch of the cubic nullcline ("quasi-threshold") [@fitzhugh1961impulses].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-threshold
#| fig-cap: "FitzHugh-Nagumo model at rest (I_app = 0, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 0.5, epsilon = 0.01). Initial kicks v(0) of 0.05 and 0.11 decay; kicks of 0.2 and 0.3 produce a full spike before returning to rest."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

from amlab.odes_2d.fitzhugh_nagumo import fitzhugh_nagumo

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
for v0 in [0.05, 0.11, 0.2, 0.3]:
    sol = solve_ivp(fitzhugh_nagumo, (0, 3), [v0, 0.0], args=(0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01),
                    max_step=0.005)
    ax.plot(sol.t, sol.y[0], label=f"v(0) = {v0}")
ax.set_xlabel("t")
ax.set_ylabel("v")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The response is all or nothing: the spikes started from $v(0) = 0.2$ and $0.3$ have almost the same height, far above the size of the kick.

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise
In @fig-threshold the rest state is $(v, w) = (0, 0)$. Use the Jacobian to show that it is stable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
With $f(v) = v(1-v)(v - \alpha)$, $f'(0) = -\alpha$. The Jacobian at the origin is $\begin{pmatrix} -\alpha/\epsilon & -1/\epsilon \\ 1 & -\gamma \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -10 & -100 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, with $\tau = -10.5 < 0$ and $\Delta = 5 + 100 > 0$. The origin is stable. Excitability is a global property: it cannot be seen in the linearization.
:::
